instruction: Guide me on how to make the terminal font size stay at 14 after rebooting, instead of resetting to default.

command: import pyautogui; import time; pyautogui.click({SCREEN_WIDTH_HALF}, {SCREEN_HEIGHT_HALF}); time.sleep(0.5);

import pyautogui; import time; time.sleep(0.5); pyautogui.hotkey('ctrl', 'alt', 't'); time.sleep(1); pyautogui.write('gsettings get org.gnome.Terminal.Legacy.Profile:/org/gnome/terminal/legacy/profiles:/:$(gsettings get org.gnome.Terminal.ProfilesList default | tr -d "'"')/ font'); time.sleep(0.5); pyautogui.press('enter')

metadata.explanation: Task requires user to persistently set terminal font size to 14. The evaluator opens a new terminal and checks the font setting using gsettings command. Expected output should contain '14' indicating font size 14 is set. Similar pattern to original task (checking terminal configuration persistence).
metadata.verification: Verified that gsettings command will return font string containing size '14' when properly configured. The postconfig executes gsettings to retrieve the font configuration from the default terminal profile.

llm_judge_reasons: Evaluator correctly verifies persistent terminal font configuration using gsettings command
Metric properly handles expected parameter for type='rule' (directly accesses expected.get('include'))
Postconfig appropriately opens fresh terminal and queries persistent configuration
Getter correctly retrieves terminal output containing font configuration
String inclusion check ('14' in output) is appropriate for this verification task
Minor risk: substring matching could theoretically produce false positives (e.g., 'Monospace 141'), though unlikely given typical gsettings output format ('Monospace 14')
llm_judge_fix_suggestions: Consider more precise regex matching (e.g., '\b14\b') to avoid false positives from numbers like 140, 141, though current approach is acceptable given typical gsettings font output format
